Section ids are kept from the German list: schwach = regular (-er, -ir like finir, -re like vendre), stark = irregular, gemischt = spelling-change -er verbs (docs/content-plan.md §3.1). The forms column is the je form without the pronoun (ai = j'ai), the il form of the passé composé with its auxiliary, and the participle; the worksheet and the live quiz read the three forms in this order. 1990 spellings and Québec differences go in the note field.
title: Regular and irregular verbs
metaTitle: Irregular French verbs list: present, passé composé and participle – Reference – icanspeak French
description: Regular, irregular and spelling-change French verbs at a glance: the je form of the present, the il form of the passé composé with avoir or être, and the past participle, grouped by pattern.
lead: Three forms tell you most of what you need about a French verb: je in the present, il in the passé composé (which also shows avoir or être), and the past participle. Verbs that change in the same way are grouped together.
practice: Practise the passé composé with avoir
Practise the passé composé with être

sections.name: Regular verbs
sections.what: Take the ending off the infinitive (-er, -ir, -re) and add the endings of its group. Nine French verbs out of ten end in -er and work like parler, and new verbs do too: liker, il a liké.
regel: Pattern: *parler: parle · a parlé · parlé.* *finir: finis · a fini · fini.* *vendre: vends · a vendu · vendu.*
In speech *je parle, tu parles, il parle, ils parlent* all sound the same: the endings are only written.
-ir verbs like *finir* add *-iss-* in the plural: *nous finissons, vous finissez, ils finissent.*
-re verbs like *vendre* have no ending in the il form: *il vend, il attend, il répond.* Grammar books count them in the third group, but they follow one pattern.
Most verbs take *avoir* in the passé composé. A small group of verbs of movement and change takes *être*, and the participle then agrees: *Elle est arrivée. Ils sont restés.*

sections.name: Irregular verbs
sections.what: Their stem changes, often in the present and in the participle. They are few, but they are the most common verbs of the language, so learn their forms by heart.
regel: The four you need first: *être: suis · a été · été*, *avoir: ai · a eu · eu*, *aller: vais · est allé · allé*, *faire: fais · a fait · fait.*
Many irregular participles end in *-u* (*vu, voulu, pu, su, lu, bu, venu*), others in *-i, -is, -it* (*dormi, pris, mis, dit, écrit*) or *-ert* (*ouvert, offert*).
Verbs built on the same verb share its forms: *prendre, apprendre, comprendre: pris, appris, compris*; *venir, devenir, revenir: venu, devenu, revenu.*
*venir, partir, sortir, naître, mourir* and their family take *être*: *Elle est partie. Il est né à Lille.*
Some take *avoir* or *être* by meaning: *Elle est sortie.* (went out) / *Elle a sorti la poubelle.* (took out)

sections.name: Spelling-change -er verbs
sections.what: Regular -er verbs whose stem changes in writing to keep the sound: an accent, a doubled consonant, ç, ge, or y becoming i. The endings and the participle stay regular.
regel: *-cer* and *-ger*: before *a* and *o*, *c* becomes *ç* and *g* becomes *ge*: *nous commençons, nous mangeons, je mangeais.*
*e* or *é* in the last syllable of the stem becomes *è* before a silent ending: *j'achète, je préfère*, but *nous achetons, nous préférons.*
*appeler* and *jeter* double the consonant instead: *j'appelle, je jette*, but *nous appelons.* Other *-eler, -eter* verbs may take *è* in the 1990 spelling: *je renouvelle / je renouvèle.*
*-oyer* and *-uyer* change *y* to *i* before a silent ending: *j'envoie, je nettoie.* With *-ayer* both are correct: *je paie / je paye.*
The participle is always regular: *commencé, acheté, appelé, payé.*
